content: The balance of benefits and harms associated with device-based voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is not favorable due to higher costs and increased safety concerns. Some stakeholders, including adolescents, adult males, their partners, communities, health policymakers, and healthcare funding organizations, may find device-based VMMC morally, religiously, or ethically unacceptable. A total of 20 studies were reviewed to assess the acceptability of device-based VMMC. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Kenya, Mozambique, Zambia, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Malawi, and South Africa. The most commonly used devices were PrePex (13 studies) and ShangRing (7 studies), with one study using the Alisklamp device. Data collection occurred between 2011 and 2014, primarily involving participants aged 18 to 54 years. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 50 to 2,250 participants, with study group ages spanning from 10 to 54 years. Two studies specifically assessed the acceptability of device-based VMMC among adolescent boys, while 19 studies focused on adult males. Five of these studies also evaluated the acceptability of device-based VMMC among healthcare providers. However, no data were available from female sexual partners, communities, policymakers, or funders. No significant methodological limitations or threats to the generalizability of the findings were identified. However, four studies had unclear reporting of methods used to assess acceptability, which did not compromise the validity of the findings. Adolescent boys reported satisfaction rates of 1% being very or extremely satisfied at 14 and 60 days post-device application. Barriers to uptake included pain, healing time, and time off from work or school. Disruptions to daily routines, such as difficulty sitting, walking, sleeping, doing housework, participating in sports, and attending school, were also noted. Preferences for procedure types varied, with 26% of Zambian respondents aged 10-14 years choosing surgical VMMC, 36% preferring PrePex, 16% preferring ShangRing, and 23% preferring Unicirc. Among adult males, high satisfaction rates were reported for both PrePex and surgical VMMC. For example, 99% of PrePex users and 100% of surgical VMMC users were satisfied with the aesthetic outcomes. Barriers included pain during the procedure, device wear period, device removal, and healing time. Other barriers included discomfort during erections, odor, hygiene maintenance difficulties, urination issues, lengthy procedure times, safety concerns, long healing times, and inconvenience due to follow-up visits or device removal. Healthcare providers highlighted the ease and simplicity of device-based VMMC as a key facilitator. For instance, providers in rural Malawi found PrePex placement easier than surgery in small treatment areas. However, barriers included perceived pain associated with the ShangRing device and slow healing processes. The existing evidence suggests that device-based VMMC is generally acceptable among adolescent and adult males. However, perspectives from female sexual partners, communities, policymakers, and funders remain unknown. Further research is warranted to gather insights from these stakeholders. Cost analyses of device-based VMMC revealed higher costs compared to conventional surgical VMMC, primarily due to disposable medical supplies and personnel costs. Seven cost-analysis studies conducted in eastern and southern Africa (Kenya, Mozambique, Uganda, South Africa, and Zambia) reported unit costs ranging from $21 to $65. The largest contributors to unit costs were consumables and staff expenses. Despite higher costs, device-based VMMC offers advantages such as shorter procedure times and fewer complications, which may offset some of the cost differences in specific contexts.
